questions.stem: When a body executing SHM is at its extreme position (maximum displacement from equilibrium), what is its instantaneous velocity?

options.option_text: Equal to ωA, same as the maximum velocity reached at mean position
Zero, because all mechanical energy is stored as potential energy here
Equal to half of ωA, as it is midway through a complete quarter-cycle
Maximum, because the restoring force has done maximum work on the body

questions.explanation: B is correct. Velocity in SHM is v = ω√(A² − x²). At the extreme position x = A, so v = ω√(A² − A²) = 0. All the energy is stored as elastic/gravitational potential energy. Option A confuses the extreme position with the mean position, where velocity is actually ωA (maximum). Option C incorrectly halves the speed with no physical basis.

questions.stem: At the mean (equilibrium) position of a body in SHM, which statement correctly describes the energy distribution?

options.option_text: Potential energy is at maximum and kinetic energy is exactly zero
Both KE and PE are each equal to half of the total mechanical energy
Kinetic energy is at its maximum value and potential energy is zero
Total mechanical energy is at its minimum value at the mean position

questions.explanation: C is correct. PE in SHM = ½mω²x². At mean position x = 0, so PE = 0. Since total energy E = ½mω²A² is conserved, all energy is kinetic: KE = E = ½mω²A² (maximum). Option A describes the extreme position, not the mean. Option B (equal split) occurs only at x = A/√2. Option D is wrong because total mechanical energy is constant throughout SHM.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum is oscillating inside a lift that is accelerating upward at 5 m/s². How does its time period compare to when the lift is stationary (take g = 10 m/s²)?

options.option_text: Increase, because effective gravity decreases inside an upward-moving lift
Stay unchanged, as gravitational acceleration acts independently of the lift
Decrease, because effective gravity increases when the lift accelerates upward
Double in value, because both gravity and inertial reaction both act on the bob

questions.explanation: C is correct. Inside an upward-accelerating lift, the effective gravitational acceleration is g_eff = g + a = 10 + 5 = 15 m/s². Since T = 2π√(L/g_eff), a larger g_eff gives a smaller T — the pendulum swings faster. Option A is the classic confusion: students mix up upward lift (g increases) with downward lift or free fall (g decreases). Option D is wrong because the period changes by a factor of √(10/15) = √(2/3), not halves.

questions.stem: Two springs, each of spring constant k, are joined in parallel and carry a mass m. If one of the springs is replaced by a spring of constant 3k (still in parallel), the new angular frequency of oscillation compared to the original is:

options.option_text: √2 times the original, since total k rises from 2k to 4k doubling the ratio
Twice the original angular frequency, as k_eff quadruples from 2k to 4k (√4 = 2)
√2 times the original value, as k_eff goes from 2k to 4k and ω ∝ √k_eff
Three times the original, since the replaced spring has triple the stiffness value

questions.explanation: C is correct. For springs in parallel, k_eff = sum of all k values. Originally k_eff = k + k = 2k. After replacing one spring: k_eff = k + 3k = 4k. Angular frequency ω = √(k_eff/m), so ω_new/ω_old = √(4k/2k) = √2. Option B mistakes ω ∝ k_eff (linear) for ω ∝ √k_eff (square root). Option A gives the right ratio √2 but wrong reasoning (k does not 'double the ratio'). Option D ignores that only one spring changed.

questions.stem: A pendulum clock keeps correct time at sea level. When transported to a high-altitude hill station where g is measurably smaller, what will the clock do?

options.option_text: Run fast, since thinner air at altitude reduces air resistance on the bob
Run slow, because reduced g increases the time period of each swing
Keep correct time, since only the string length and bob mass determine T
Run fast initially, then self-correct as the bob adjusts to the new gravity

questions.explanation: B is correct. T = 2π√(L/g). At higher altitude g decreases, so T increases — each swing takes longer, meaning the clock completes fewer oscillations per hour and loses time (runs slow). Option A confuses air resistance (a minor secondary effect) with the dominant gravitational effect, and also gets the direction wrong. Option C is wrong because g is explicitly part of the formula. Option D is a fabrication — pendula have no self-correction mechanism for gravity change.

questions.stem: A particle in SHM has amplitude A and total mechanical energy E. At displacement x = A√3/2 from the mean position, what fraction of E is kinetic energy?

options.option_text: 3E/4, because PE = (3/4)E at this displacement leaving only one-quarter as KE
E/4, since KE = E − PE = E − ½mω²(3A²/4) = E/4 at x = A√3/2
E/2, because the displacement A√3/2 is roughly the midpoint between 0 and A
√3E/2, obtained by applying the displacement ratio directly to total energy

questions.explanation: B is correct. Total energy E = ½mω²A². At x = A√3/2, PE = ½mω²x² = ½mω²·(3A²/4) = (3/4)·½mω²A² = 3E/4. Therefore KE = E − PE = E − 3E/4 = E/4. Option A reverses KE and PE — a common mistake where students assign (3/4)E to KE instead of PE. Option C is incorrect because x = A√3/2 ≈ 0.866A, far from the midpoint. Option D wrongly applies a linear scaling rule instead of the squared displacement relationship.

questions.stem: The bob of a simple pendulum is replaced with one of double the mass, and simultaneously the string length is reduced to one-quarter of its original value. If the original time period was T, the new time period is:

options.option_text: T/2, because halving the effective length reduces time period by factor of two
T/√2, since only length changes by factor of 4 and gives √4 = 2 reduction
T/(2√2), as both doubling mass and quartering length together reduce T further
T/4, because quartering the string length quarters the resulting time period too

questions.explanation: A is correct. T = 2π√(L/g); mass does not appear in this formula — doubling the bob's mass has absolutely zero effect on T. With L reduced to L/4: T_new = 2π√(L/4 / g) = 2π·(1/2)·√(L/g) = T/2. Option B gives the correct ratio T/2 but with garbled reasoning (it claims √4 = 2 reduction of length by 'factor 2', confusing length change with period change). Option C is the most tempting wrong answer — examinees mistakenly apply mass to the formula as √(mass) scaling. Option D confuses T ∝ √L with T ∝ L, giving a linear (wrong) relationship.

questions.stem: In Simple Harmonic Motion, what is the phase difference between the displacement and the velocity of the oscillating particle?

options.option_text: 0° — displacement and velocity are perfectly in phase always
180° (π rad) — they are always exactly opposite in direction
90° (π/2 rad) — velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle
45° (π/4 rad) — they are separated by one-eighth of a full cycle

questions.explanation: C is correct. If displacement x = A sin(ωt), then velocity v = Aω cos(ωt) = Aω sin(ωt + π/2), so velocity leads displacement by exactly π/2 (90°). Option B is the most tempting wrong answer — a phase difference of 180° applies between displacement and acceleration (since a = −ω²x), not between displacement and velocity.

questions.stem: In a spring-mass system with spring constant k, the attached mass m is doubled while k remains unchanged. What happens to the time period of oscillation?

options.option_text: remains unchanged, as mass does not affect spring-mass oscillation
increases by a factor of √2 (approximately 1.41 times the original)
doubles to exactly twice the original time period of oscillation
halves to exactly half the original time period of oscillation

questions.explanation: B is correct. T = 2π√(m/k). When m → 2m: T_new = 2π√(2m/k) = T√2 ≈ 1.41T. Option A is the classic confusion with simple pendulums, whose period is mass-independent; for spring-mass systems T ∝ √m. Option C is wrong because T ∝ √m not m — doubling m gives T√2, not 2T.

questions.stem: A spring of constant k oscillates a block of mass m with time period T. The spring is cut into two equal halves and the same block is attached to one half only. What is the new time period?

options.option_text: T/√2 — the stiffer half-spring reduces the time period of oscillation
T·√2 — shorter spring vibrates slower due to reduced restoring force
T/2 — period halves exactly because the spring length is exactly halved
T unchanged — cutting the spring length does not alter its spring constant

questions.explanation: A is correct. For a uniform spring, k ∝ 1/L. Halving the length doubles the spring constant to 2k. New T = 2π√(m/2k) = T/√2 ≈ 0.707T. Option D is the most common error — students assume spring constant is a material property alone. Option C confuses T ∝ (1/k)^(1/2) with a direct inverse relationship between T and L.

questions.stem: In SHM with amplitude A, when a particle's displacement from the equilibrium position is A/2, what is the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy?

options.option_text: 1:1 — energy distributes equally at exactly half the amplitude value
1:3 — potential energy dominates at half-amplitude displacement point
√3:1 — derived from square root of the displacement-to-amplitude ratio
3:1 — kinetic energy is three times the potential energy at this point

questions.explanation: D is correct. PE = ½mω²x² = ½mω²(A/2)² = mω²A²/8. Total energy E = ½mω²A². KE = E − PE = 4mω²A²/8 − mω²A²/8 = 3mω²A²/8. So KE:PE = 3:1. Option A (1:1 ratio) only holds at x = A/√2 ≈ 0.707A, a completely different displacement. Option B (1:3) would require the particle to be beyond x = A/√2, not at A/2.

questions.stem: A pendulum clock keeps accurate time at 20°C. The temperature rises to 40°C and the metallic pendulum rod expands thermally. What effect does this have on the clock's timekeeping?

options.option_text: loses time, as the longer rod increases the time period of oscillation
gains time, since higher temperature speeds up the molecular oscillations
keeps accurate time since pendulum clocks auto-compensate for heat expansion
loses time only if the rod is brass; steel rods remain thermally stable

questions.explanation: A is correct. T = 2π√(L/g). Thermal expansion increases L (ΔL/L = αΔT), so T increases and the pendulum completes fewer oscillations per day — the clock loses time. Option D is wrong because ALL common metals (steel, brass, iron) have positive linear expansion coefficients and all cause the clock to run slow. Compensation requires special near-zero-α alloys like invar.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum (mass m, string length L) is released from rest at angle θ from the vertical. What is the ratio of string tension at the lowest point to string tension at the highest turning point?

options.option_text: (3 − 2cosθ)/cosθ — derived via energy conservation and centripetal law
cosθ/(3 − 2cosθ) — the inverse, obtained by swapping the two tension values
(1 + 2cosθ)/cosθ — uses incorrect velocity expression at the mean position
(3 + 2cosθ)/(1 + cosθ) — adds instead of subtracting cosθ in the numerator

questions.explanation: A is correct. At the highest point (v = 0): centripetal condition gives T_top − mg cosθ = 0, so T_top = mg cosθ. At the lowest point: energy conservation gives v² = 2gL(1−cosθ); centripetal condition gives T_bot − mg = mv²/L = 2mg(1−cosθ), so T_bot = mg(3−2cosθ). Ratio = (3−2cosθ)/cosθ. Option C uses v² = gL(1−cosθ) instead of 2gL(1−cosθ) — a factor-of-2 slip in applying the work-energy theorem.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum with natural time period T is suspended in a vehicle that accelerates horizontally at a = g m/s² (equal in magnitude to gravitational acceleration). The new time period of the pendulum is?

options.option_text: T/√2 ≈ 0.707T — effective g doubles so period reduces by factor root-two
T·√2 ≈ 1.414T — horizontal force opposes gravity, reducing net downward g
T/2^(1/4) ≈ 0.841T — effective g becomes g√2 and T scales as g^(−1/2)
T/2 = 0.500T — effective g equals 2g so the period becomes exactly half T

questions.explanation: C is correct. Horizontal acceleration a = g is perpendicular to gravity g, so effective gravity g_eff = √(g² + g²) = g√2 (vector sum, not scalar sum). New period T_new = 2π√(L/g√2) = T·(1/√2)^(1/2) = T/2^(1/4) ≈ 0.841T. Option A error: assumes g_eff = 2g (scalar addition) instead of the correct vector magnitude g√2. Option D error: uses T ∝ 1/g_eff (linear) instead of the correct T ∝ g_eff^(−1/2).
